messages.content: Respond to a fictional educational clinical case for a research evaluation. Follow the stated task and audience. Use only the supplied patient facts and conversation. Distinguish facts from hypotheses and make uncertainty explicit. Give concise final clinical justifications, not a private internal reasoning trace.

Case facts:
Basic patient information: 36-year-old woman.
Consultation context: The current consultation is the readmission beginning 14 March 2026. The earlier admission ended on 11 March 2026. No later recurrence or additional admission is being simulated.
Only existing selected records are available. Unreported information remains unknown, not normal, negative or evidence that a test was never performed. Do not infer an exact test/report time when none is given. Later diagnoses and outcomes are withheld.
Patient opening:
My severe headache has returned and is worse when I am upright.

Task:
Audience: the treating clinical team. Write 160–230 words in English. Start with a one-sentence summary of the main clinical problem. Prioritise up to three working explanations, explaining the supporting findings, limitations and useful next information for each. Consider the history, treatment and investigation information actually supplied together. Identify any clinical reassessment needed before deciding management. Give concise clinical justifications. Do not invent unreported results or treat a negative investigation as excluding every cause. Do not prescribe exact drug doses or claim a final diagnosis from information not supplied.

Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.

Earlier conversation (context):
Clinician: Can you tell me more about this headache — when it started this time, how it has changed since your recent admission, and any other symptoms that came with it?
Patient: The headache and sensitivity to light persisted, and I returned to emergency care. I was readmitted on 14 March with a severe headache when upright, tremor in my arms and dizziness.

Clinician: During your first admission, what tests or procedures were done — for example, did you have a lumbar puncture, and what was the diagnosis you were given at discharge?
Fixed clinical record [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.]: Her past medical history was unremarkable.
Fixed clinical record [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.]: Initial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) contained 183 cells/µL, 97.8% lymphocytes, and protein 83.3 mg/dL.

Fixed clinical record [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.]: head CT showed no abnormality.

Clinician: Were any infection tests done on your first admission — for example PCR or serology on the spinal fluid or blood — and what were the results?
Fixed clinical record [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.]: CSF PCR did not identify an infectious cause, and Borrelia serology was negative. No CSF culture result is supplied.

message.content:
**Summary:** A 36-year-old woman is readmitted three days after discharge with recurrent severe orthostatic headache, photophobia, tremor and dizziness, following a first admission showing lymphocytic meningitis (CSF 183 cells/µL, 97.8% lymphocytes, protein 83.3 mg/dL).

**Working explanations:**

1. **Post-dural-puncture or low-pressure headache:** The marked worsening when upright is the classic pattern. A lumbar puncture was performed; timing relative to symptom onset is not supplied, so causality is uncertain. A normal head CT does not exclude this. Useful next information: exact LP date, need for repeat imaging (MRI with contrast or CT myelography) to look for dural leak.

2. **Relapsing or incompletely treated aseptic meningitis:** CSF pleocytosis with negative infectious PCR and Borrelia serology leaves many causes unexcluded; no culture result is supplied. Recurrence after steroid cessation (dexamethasone for nine days) could reflect rebound of an inflammatory process. Useful next information: repeat CSF analysis, autoimmune/other infective workup.

3. **Steroid-withdrawal effect:** Dexamethasone stopped around discharge; headache, tremor and dizziness may partly reflect withdrawal, though this would not fully explain orthostatic worsening.

**Reassessment needed:** Full neurological examination, vital signs including postural blood pressure, and medication review before deciding management. No final diagnosis can be assigned from the supplied information.
